title: Reading slump with Mia
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex and Mia admit to a reading slump, weigh audiobooks against paper and listening on easy runs, compare the absurdism of Camus' The Stranger with Stoicism, and defer choosing next month's book until the end, when they pick Seneca's letters.

utterances.text: Okay, confession before we start. I haven't read anything in three weeks.
Oh, thank goodness. Me neither. Well, I finished The Stranger, barely, and nothing since.
A slump! Both of us. Book club in crisis.
It's the new job. I get home and my brain is foam board. I read the same paragraph four times.
Mine's just my phone. I pick it up to check the time and suddenly it's midnight.
So much for our rule. Paper only, phones in the other room.
I've been thinking about audiobooks. Is that cheating?
I used to think so. But honestly, I listened to half of The Stranger as an audiobook.
Wait, really? You, the margin scribbler?
I know. But I listen on my easy runs now. Jordan wants them slow, and a story stops me speeding up.
Oh, that's smart. Music makes you race, a book makes you chill.
Exactly. Forty minutes of Camus at six fifteen pace.
Do you remember it as well as paper?
Not really. I hear a great line, then I'm crossing a road and it's gone.
So maybe audiobooks for stories, paper for the stuff you want to keep.
That's a good rule. Okay, can we talk about The Stranger? I need to talk about the ending.
Yes. The prison chapter, when he finally explodes at the chaplain.
And then he's calm, because he accepts that the world doesn't care about him. I got chills on a run.
Last time I said it's the opposite of Marcus Aurelius. Do you still think so?
Kind of the opposite, kind of not. They both say the universe doesn't care what you want.
Right, but the Stoics think there's a rational order to it, and you fit in by doing your duty.
And Camus says there's no order at all. That's the absurd. You want meaning, the world stays silent, and you live anyway.
So Stoicism is accept your place, and absurdism is there is no place, make your own.
Pretty much. Marcus gets up for his duty. Meursault goes swimming.
Okay, what are we reading next month? Actually, let's pick next month's book later, I want to think.
Sure, later. Weirdly, the slump feels better just from talking about it.
That's the whole point of a two-person book club with a cheese plate.
Okay, it's later. Next month's book. Seneca, Letters from a Stoic. They're short, like a page each. Perfect for a slump.
Another Stoic? You're obsessed. But fine, a warmer one. Paper, one letter a night, before bed.
